note.explanation: A magnet points north–south when freely suspended. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Attraction alone cannot prove that an object is a magnet: it may be a magnetic material. Repulsion by one pole of a suspended magnet is the real test.
examples: Bring an unknown object near the north pole of a suspended magnet. If it is attracted, it might be a south pole or a magnetic material.
Bring the same end near the south pole. If it is repelled, the object is a magnet; if it is attracted again, it is a magnetic material.
note.simple: Attraction does not prove an object is a magnet. Repulsion does.
note.checkQuestion: What happens when unlike poles are brought near each other?
note.title: Properties of Magnets
steps: Bring one end of the object near a pole of a suspended magnet.
If it is attracted, test the same end against the other pole.
If attracted by both poles, the object is a magnetic material.
If repelled by the other pole, the object is a magnet.
note.answer: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Repulsion between like poles is the real test for identifying a magnet.

mcqs.stem: What is the name of the end of a freely suspended bar magnet that points north?
rationales: Correct: the end that points north is called the north magnetic pole.
Incorrect: the south magnetic pole is the end that points south.
Incorrect: the pole is named by the direction it points, not by its colour.
Incorrect: the north-pointing end is identified as a magnetic pole.

options: They have no effect on one another.
mcqs.stem: What happens when the north poles of two magnets are brought near each other?
rationales: Correct: like poles repel, so two north poles repel.
Incorrect: attraction occurs between unlike poles.
Incorrect: the section states that like poles interact by repelling.
Incorrect: bringing poles together does not turn them into magnetic materials.

mcqs.stem: What happens when the south poles of two magnets are brought near each other?
rationales: Correct: two south poles are like poles, and like poles repel.
Incorrect: unlike poles attract; two south poles are alike.
Incorrect: pointing north is a property of a freely suspended magnet, not the interaction of two south poles.
Incorrect: bringing like poles together does not make the magnets lose their poles.

options: They have no effect on one another.
mcqs.stem: What happens when a north pole is brought near a south pole?
rationales: Correct: unlike poles attract.
Incorrect: repulsion occurs between like poles.
Incorrect: the section states that unlike poles attract.
Incorrect: bringing unlike poles together does not change either pole into a north pole.

options: Attraction by either pole of a suspended magnet

mcqs.stem: Which observation is the real test for identifying an object as a magnet?
rationales: Incorrect: a magnetic material can also be attracted, so attraction alone is not a sure test.
Correct: repulsion by a like pole confirms that the object is a magnet.
Incorrect: colour does not identify a magnet.
Incorrect: weight does not identify a magnet.

options: It is a magnetic material, not a magnet.
mcqs.stem: An unknown object is attracted to both ends of a suspended bar magnet. What can you conclude?
rationales: Correct: attraction by both poles indicates a magnetic material rather than a magnet.
Incorrect: attraction alone cannot prove that the object is a magnet.
Incorrect: the observation does not identify the object as a south pole.
Incorrect: testing it against both poles gives a conclusion.

options: Each piece has both a north pole and a south pole.
One piece has only a north pole and the other only a south pole.
Only the larger piece remains magnetic.
mcqs.stem: What happens when a bar magnet is broken into two pieces?
rationales: Correct: each piece is a complete magnet with both poles.
Incorrect: the section says isolated north and south poles cannot be obtained by breaking a magnet.
Incorrect: both pieces have two poles, regardless of their size.
Incorrect: each piece remains a complete magnet.

explain.title: A suspended magnet points north–south
explain.body: If a bar magnet is suspended horizontally through a string and allowed to come to rest, it will point in north-south direction. The end of the magnet that points north is called the north magnetic pole (N) and the end that points south is the south magnetic pole (S).

explain.title: How poles interact
explain.body: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Two north poles repel; two south poles repel; a north pole and a south pole attract.

explain.title: How to identify a magnet
explain.body: If the same end of an unknown object is attracted by both ends of a suspended magnet, it is a magnetic material. If it is repelled by the other end, it is a magnet. The repulsion between the like poles is a real test to identify a magnet.

explain.title: A magnet always has two poles
explain.body: Breaking a bar magnet does not give separate north and south poles. Each piece will have its two poles, i.e., N-pole and S-pole. Even if a magnet is divided into thousands pieces, each piece will be a complete magnet with its N, and S-poles.

mistakes: Do not say that attraction alone proves an object is a magnet; magnetic materials are also attracted.
Do not mix up the pole rule: like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
Do not call the end that points south the north pole.
Do not claim that breaking a magnet separates its north and south poles; each piece has both poles.
When describing the identification test, test the same end of the object against the other pole.
